headline: Citizen Scientists Spot Rare Wasp on Social Media, Help Scientists Make Discovery
meta_description: Japanese wasp enthusiasts' social media posts led to the first recording of Eupelmus curvator in Japan and the first scientific description of the species' mal…
summary_short: Striking wasp photos posted on Twitter by Japanese enthusiasts became the first record of the species in Japan—and helped scientists describe the male for the first time.
body:
When wasp enthusiasts in Japan shared photos and videos of a striking, iridescent insect on social media in 2018 and 2021, they set in motion an unexpected discovery. Taisuke Kawano, a wasp expert at the Kyushu University Museum, noticed the footage and reached out to the citizen scientists. What followed was the first recorded sighting of Eupelmus curvator in Japan—and the first scientific description of the species' male, previously unknown to science. The videos showed something remarkable: a female wasp depositing her eggs directly into the egg case of a praying mantis, a behavior that parasitoid wasps use to ensure their developing larvae have a ready food source.

The researchers identified the species and worked with the original citizen scientists, making them co-authors of a study published in June. The findings revealed the wasp's new reach—Eupelmus curvator was previously known only from China. In one mantis egg case studied, scientists found 77 wasps and just a few surviving mantis babies, illustrating the species' efficiency as a parasitoid. The wasp was also recorded targeting the eggs of the narrow-winged mantis for the first time.

Kawano emphasizes that social media's power lies not in replacing traditional research, but in expanding it. "Social media can be particularly useful for detecting unusual behavior, host associations, or records from previously undocumented regions," he explained. Specimens remain essential for accurate identification, especially with microscopic insects, but digital observations create starting points that field surveys alone might miss. With entomologists estimating up to a million parasitoid wasp species still undescribed, tools like social media may prove increasingly vital for unlocking nature's hidden diversity.
quick_facts: First record of Eupelmus curvator parasitoid wasp in Japan, previously known only from China
Citizen scientists posted wasp photos on Twitter in 2018 and 2021
One mantis egg case contained 77 wasps and only a few surviving mantis babies
Study published in June; citizen scientists became co-authors of the research
